note: Two-lens rubrics survey for IDEAS.md §7.3. 8 agents (3 web research, 5 fleet readers) surveyed 6 repos and 3 open-web domains. Core finding: rubrics-as-constraint-graphs is a genuine unfilled gap. The fleet has rich rubric structures under other names. The open world is converging (RADAR, OpenRubrics, Checkov, OPA) but no shipping tool combines rubric-criteria-as-DAG with human-sealed-verdicts. Nestor's decision-edge covenant — 4 typed edges, constraints_on(question) traversal, propose-never-confirm — is already that tool, unrecognized. All findings are proposed, none sealed — a survey is evidence for a human to weigh at nestor ui.

decisions.question: Is a rubric a domain the decision recipe already answers, or a shape that needs its own machinery?
decisions.commitment: Neither — it is the decision graph read as what it already is. constraints_on(question) at decision.py:196 is rubric evaluation: 'score this proposal against the criteria that touch it.' The 4 edge types (supersedes, refines, depends_on, contradicts) are the inter-criterion dependencies every graph-shaped rubric in the survey models. A rubric is not new machinery bolted beside the decision store; it is a view of the store. The fleet's assessment-visibility E1→E4 dependency graph (CC BY 4.0), willow-gate's trust ladder (Apache 2.0), prod-readiness's no-go gates (MIT), and the open world's Checkov policy-DAG and OPA/Rego rule-DAG (both Apache 2.0) all model criteria-as-graph — and none combine it with human-sealed verdicts. Nestor already does.
decisions.why: The survey's convergence matrix is the evidence: 9 sources surveyed, all model some subset of {criteria-as-graph, human-seal, traversal}, Nestor is the only one with all three. This is not argued from first principles; it is observed across 6 fleet repos and 3 web domains. The flat-scorecard model (dominant in education) is the degenerate zero-edge case — already superseded by the edge covenant. The 'rubric view' implementation is a downstream build question; this decision records the survey finding that settles §7.3 question 1.
decisions.doors_closed: A rubric as a new recipe or domain requiring new machinery distinct from the decision-edge covenant. A flat-scorecard model (independent criteria, no inter-criterion constraints) as the rubric shape — the survey shows the graph shape is the convergence point, and Nestor already has it.

decisions.question: Which fleet and open-world rubric structures are re-landable into Apache-2.0, and what gates them?
decisions.commitment: Structure re-lands (clean): Checkov's policy-DAG meta-model (Apache 2.0); OPA/Rego's rule-dependency DAG (Apache 2.0); assessment-visibility's E1→E4 dependency-graph shape and false-negative pattern table (CC BY 4.0, attribution required); willow-gate's trust-ladder rung-gating pattern (Apache 2.0); prod-readiness's no-go gates and conditional activation (MIT). Ideas-only re-lands (clean-room): RADAR's inter-criterion dependency model (academic); OpenRubrics' hard-rule/soft-principle split (open/permissive); terpsi-music's anchor-type constraints (license unstated). Two gates: the license gate (permissive → text, share-alike or none → ideas-only, clean-room) and an ethical gate on assessment-visibility and terpsi-music (education/minors — re-land structure only, never domain content or student-facing vocabulary).
decisions.why: The license gate is the standard IDEAS §7.3 names; it was applied identically to every source. The ethical gate on education content is named separately because it is stricter than the license allows — CC BY 4.0 legally permits verbatim re-use with attribution, but the domain (minors' records, classroom contexts) makes content re-landing irresponsible even when legal. Recording both gates keeps the re-land inventory honest about what stops each item.
decisions.doors_closed: Verbatim re-landing of education-domain content from assessment-visibility or terpsi-music, even where the license would permit it (ethical gate, not legal). Treating the license gate as the only gate — the ethical constraint is independent and stricter.

decisions.question: Does the survey strengthen the case for a conflict-scan (§7.3 question 2) and inter-rater reliability integration?
decisions.commitment: Both strengthened, neither built. Conflict-scan: Checkov and OPA both traverse policy graphs to find contradictions — the same operation a contradicts-edge traversal of the decision graph would perform. The rubric-self-contradiction defect documented in decision 0084 is exactly the failure mode this traversal catches. Inter-rater reliability: the education literature's kappa/alpha measures (do two raters applying the same rubric agree?) map directly to Nestor's matcher precision problem. This reframes nestor calibrate as rubric calibration — the same problem with a longer literature and a richer toolkit. Both are downstream build questions; the survey provides evidence, not implementations.
decisions.why: Recording the evidence separately from the build commitment keeps the decision honest — the survey found supporting evidence for both ideas, but neither has been built or tested. The conflict-scan evidence is structural (two shipping tools already traverse policy graphs for contradictions); the inter-rater reliability evidence is conceptual (the mapping between kappa and matcher precision is an idea, not code). Both need their own decisions when they are built.
decisions.doors_closed: Claiming conflict-scan or inter-rater reliability as implemented — both are strengthened hypotheses, not shipped features.
